saint.name: St. Augustine of Hippo
saint.summary: As a young man, Augustine prayed to be made pure and added two words: "not yet." He was afraid, he admitted, that God would answer too soon. He stole pears he did not want, lied to his mother on the shore at Carthage and sailed away while she prayed, and spent nine years in a sect. Then a child's voice in a garden in Milan chanted "Take up and read." The restless teacher became a priest seized by a crowd while he wept, a bishop with a verse against gossip inscribed on his table, and the author of the Confessions. How does a man who fears his own prayer become one of the great teachers of the Church?
saint.biography:
The Prayer He Feared Would Be Answered

When Augustine was still young, long before anyone thought of him as a bishop, he prayed to be made pure. He meant it, in his way. He also knew what he wanted more. Years later, when he wrote the story of his life as one long prayer to God, he set the two desires side by side in a single sentence, and no reader can miss the joke at his own expense.

“Give me chastity and continency, only not yet.”

— Augustine, Confessions, Book VIII (tr. E. B. Pusey)

Then, because he would not let himself look better than he was, he explained it. “For I feared lest Thou shouldest hear me soon.” He wanted to want God. He did not yet want God more than everything God would ask him to give up, and he knew it, and for years he lived inside that split. In those years Augustine was a gifted teacher of rhetoric, a seeker who fell in love with philosophy and joined a sect, a man who loved a woman he never married and kept the son she gave him. Through all of it his mother wept and prayed for him, and once he lied to her face to get away from her.

That young man became the bishop of Hippo, a seaport in North Africa, where he judged his people's lawsuits, kept a plain table, and preached until his last illness. He wrote the Confessions and the City of God. The Catholic Church counts him among the four great Doctors of the Latin Church, with Ambrose, Jerome, and Gregory, and by the sixth century the calendars of the churches already kept his feast. Orthodox Christians honor him as well.

How does a man who is afraid his own prayer will be answered become one of the great teachers of the Church? He gave the answer himself, on the first page of the Confessions, in a sentence addressed to God: “Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee.” Augustine's life is the story of that restless heart. He looked for rest in friendship, in love, in success, in philosophy, and in a sect, and each time he found something good and lost it again. What stood between him and God, he came to see, was his own divided will. What broke it was a child's voice in a garden in Milan. What followed was almost forty years as priest and bishop, spent giving away the very rest he had found.

It began in a small town in Numidia, with a praying mother, a hot-tempered father, and a boy who could not leave a pear tree alone.

Pears He Did Not Want

Augustine was born at Tagaste, a small town in the Roman province of Numidia, about fifty miles southeast of Hippo and about a hundred and fifty miles southwest of Carthage. The day was 13 November. He knew his birthday because he named it himself in one of his early dialogues, and his editors give the year as 354. His father, Patricius, belonged to the class of town councillors. As Augustine tells it, he did not yet share his wife's faith, and he was quick to anger; Alban Butler, writing in the eighteenth century, called him a man of “hasty choleric disposition.” His mother, Monica, was a Christian. There was a brother, Navigius, and a sister who would one day lead a community of women who served God.

The parents wanted their clever son to rise, and they paid for a liberal education. Monica wanted something more. When Augustine was a boy he fell seriously ill at school and begged to be baptized, and his mother began to prepare it. Then he recovered, and the baptism was put off. Augustine would later condemn that habit of delay. As a grown man he could see what it had cost him.

The proof, in his own telling, came in his sixteenth year. Near the family vineyard stood a pear tree heavy with fruit, though neither the look nor the taste of the pears was tempting. One night a gang of boys, Augustine among them, shook the tree and carried the fruit away. They did not want it. Some thirty years later, writing to God, he still could not leave that fact alone.

“Fair were those pears, but not them did my wretched soul desire; for I had store of better, and those I gathered, only that I might steal. For, when gathered, I flung them away, my only feast therein being my own sin.”

— Augustine, Confessions, Book II (tr. E. B. Pusey)

Plenty of boys have stolen fruit. Few have spent pages of a great book asking why. Augustine turned the night over and over, looking for the motive, and found two answers he did not like. He had loved the wrong for its own sake, and he had loved the company. “Alone I had never done it,” he wrote. A boy who steals pears to eat them is hungry. A boy who steals pears to throw them away wants something he cannot name, and that was the question Augustine carried out of Tagaste: what did he really want?

At sixteen he did not know. In a few years he would carry the question to Carthage, the great city of the province.

A Cauldron of Unholy Loves

Augustine opened the third book of the Confessions with a line that still has the heat of the city in it: “To Carthage I came, where there sang all around me in my ears a cauldron of unholy loves.” He went to the theaters. He was not yet in love with anyone, he said; he was in love with being in love. “I loved not yet, yet I loved to love.”

Before long he did love someone. He took a woman as his companion without marriage, and she bore him a son, whom they named Adeodatus. Meanwhile his father died, baptized, according to Butler and to Weiskotten's notes, shortly before the end. Augustine went on with the studies his parents had paid for, and in his nineteenth year, “my father being dead two years before,” he came upon a book by Cicero called the Hortensius. He had picked it up to sharpen his eloquence. It did something else to him. “This book altered my affections,” he wrote, “and turned my prayers to Thyself O Lord.” Every vain hope, he said, became worthless to him at once, and he longed “with an incredibly burning desire for an immortality of wisdom.”

A nineteen-year-old had fallen in love with truth itself. The trouble was where he went to look for it. He joined the Manichees, and for nine years, “from my nineteenth year to my eight-and-twentieth,” he was one of their hearers. That was the outer rank of followers; he never became one of the inner company they called the elect. He looked back on those years without mercy for himself: “we lived seduced and seducing, deceived and deceiving.” From about 374 he taught rhetoric at Carthage, and he taught it for nine years.

In those years a close friend died at Tagaste, and Augustine's world went dark. He marveled that other people, who would die too, could go on living when this friend was dead, and he marveled still more that he himself could live. He borrowed a poet's phrase for what he had lost.

“Well said one of his friend, ‘Thou half of my soul,’” he wrote, “for I felt that my soul and his soul were ‘one soul in two bodies’: and therefore was my life a horror to me, because I would not live halved.” Looking back, he could name the mistake. He had loved a man who must die as if he would never die. He had tried to build his rest on something that could not hold it.

One person refused to accept any of this as final. She had been weeping for him for years.

The Son of These Tears

Monica did not argue her son out of the Manichees. She prayed, and she wept, and one night she dreamed. In the dream she was standing on a wooden rule, a builder's straight measuring stick. A shining young man came to her and told her that where she was, there her son was also.

When she told Augustine, he saw an opening at once. Perhaps the dream meant that she would one day come over to his side. Monica did not stop to consider it. “No,” she said, “for it was not told me that, ‘where he, there thou also’; but ‘where thou, there he also.’” He made his living with words, and his mother had beaten him in one sentence. Decades later he still set down her answer word for word.

She did not stop at dreams. Monica went to a bishop and begged him to talk with her son. The bishop refused. Augustine, he said, was still unteachable. He knew what he was talking about: as a child he himself had been handed over to the Manichees by his own mother, and he had copied out their books. Monica would not take no for an answer. She pressed him with entreaties and many tears, until at last, a little displeased at her insistence, he sent her away with these words.

“Go thy ways and God bless thee, for it is not possible that the son of these tears should perish.”

— A bishop to Monica, in Augustine's Confessions, Book III (tr. E. B. Pusey)

It did not look that way for years. In time Augustine met Faustus, the famous teacher of the Manichees, and found a fine speaker whose fine speech covered weak answers. A professional teacher of rhetoric knew the difference.

About 383 he decided to leave Carthage for Rome. The pay was better there, and the students were better behaved than the rowdy set at Carthage known as the eversores, the wreckers. Monica did not want him to go, and she followed him down to the sea. Augustine told her he was only waiting to see a friend off, and that he could not leave the friend until the wind turned fair. She spent the night praying in an oratory of St. Cyprian. While she prayed, he sailed.

“And I lied to my mother,” he wrote, “and such a mother, and escaped.” He did not soften what came next. “The wind blew and swelled our sails, and withdrew the shore from our sight; and she on the morrow was there, frantic with sorrow.” Yet the bishop who wrote those words saw something the young man on the ship could not. God, he wrote, was using even his selfish wishes against him: “whilst through my desires, Thou wert hurrying me to end all desire.”

Rome went badly. He fell gravely ill there. When he recovered and began to teach, he found that the Roman students, however well behaved, found ways to avoid paying their fees. So in 384, when he was named to teach rhetoric at Milan, he went. Milan had a bishop named Ambrose.

A Bishop Reading in Silence

Augustine went to hear Ambrose preach. Possidius, his friend and biographer, says he stood among the people and listened “in eager suspense” to the sermons, more eager than others to hear whether anything would be said for or against the Manichees. In Possidius's telling, the questions of the Law that bore on that error were solved, and little by little Augustine was led on until the heresy was driven from his soul.

He wanted to speak with Ambrose alone and could hardly ever manage it. The bishop was surrounded by crowds of people with business. His door stood open to anyone, and visitors were not announced, so Augustine and his friends would come in and sit. Often they found him reading, and Augustine set down decades later exactly how he read.

“But when he was reading, his eye glided over the pages, and his heart searched out the sense, but his voice and tongue were at rest.”

— Augustine on Ambrose, Confessions, Book VI (tr. E. B. Pusey)

They would sit for a long time in silence, watching him, and then go away. Augustine made his living by talking, and the scene stayed with him. In those same Milan years he began to turn inward. “I entered even into my inward self,” he wrote, “Thou being my Guide.”

Monica had followed him to Milan. His career was rising, and a marriage was being planned for him. The woman who had shared his life since Carthage, the mother of his son, stood in the way. She was sent back to Africa. Few passages in the Confessions are as raw as the one he wrote about that parting.

“My concubine being torn from my side as a hindrance to my marriage, my heart which clave unto her was torn and wounded and bleeding. And she returned to Afric, vowing unto Thee never to know any other man, leaving with me my son by her.”

— Augustine, Confessions, Book VI (tr. E. B. Pusey)

The wedding was two years off, and in the meantime he took another woman. This was the season of the prayer he later quoted against himself, “only not yet,” and of the fear that God would hear it too soon. He wanted to be freed, and he was afraid of being freed.

Then, one day in Milan, a visitor came to the house with a story.

Take Up and Read

The year was 386, by the traditional reckoning. The visitor's name was Ponticianus, and he told Augustine and his friend Alypius the story of Antony, the monk of Egypt. Augustine turned on Alypius. “What ails us?” he cried.

He went out into the garden of the house, and he left Alypius sitting where they had been, so that he could weep alone. Under a fig tree Augustine gave way to tears. For years he had answered God with “not yet.” Now, in the middle of his weeping, he heard something.

“I heard from a neighbouring house a voice, as of boy or girl, I know not, chanting, and oft repeating, ‘Take up and read; Take up and read.’”

— Augustine, Confessions, Book VIII (tr. E. B. Pusey)

He stopped crying and tried to think. Was there some children's game in which they sang those words? He could not remember ever hearing one. He got up and went back to the seat where Alypius was sitting, where he had left a book of the letters of the Apostle Paul. Opening it, he read the first passage his eyes fell on, from the letter to the Romans: “put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh, in concupiscence.”

“No further would I read; nor needed I,” he wrote. In that instant, he said, “all the darkness of doubt vanished away.” He put his finger in the book to keep the place and shut it, and with a calm face he told Alypius what had happened. Alypius read the verse that came next, took it for himself, and joined his friend on the spot.

The prayer of “not yet” had been answered with “now.” Augustine and Alypius went into the house to find Monica. They told her, and she leapt for joy. For years she had wept for this, and the bishop had been right: the son of those tears had not perished.

A Window Over the Garden at Ostia

Augustine gave up his chair of rhetoric at the end of the vintage holidays and began to prepare for baptism. He told one small story from those months himself. He was struck by a toothache so savage that he could not speak. On a wax tablet he wrote a request that the friends around him pray for him. They knelt, he recalled, and the pain was gone.

At the beginning of Lent in 387 he came to Milan to join the candidates for baptism. On the night before Easter, Ambrose baptized him, together with Alypius and Adeodatus, who was then about fifteen. Augustine summed up the change in a single clause: “we were baptised, and anxiety for our past life vanished from us.” What he remembered most from those days was music. “How did I weep, in Thy Hymns and Canticles,” he wrote, “touched to the quick by the voices of Thy sweet-attuned Church!” The man who had wept under the fig tree in anguish now wept in church, and was happy in it.

Their friend Evodius joined them, and together they decided to go home to Africa and serve God there. On the way they came to Ostia. One day, in a house where they were staying, Augustine and his mother found themselves alone, leaning in a window that looked down into the garden. They began to talk about what the eternal life of the saints would be like.

Augustine wrote that they talked “very sweetly,” and that as they talked their minds rose step by step until they seemed to “pass through all things bodily,” even the sky itself. Then Monica spoke. “Son, for mine own part I have no further delight in any thing in this life,” she told him. “One thing there was for which I desired to linger for a while in this life, that I might see thee a Catholic Christian before I died.” God had given her that.

Five days later, or a little more, she fell ill with a fever. Once she fainted, and when she came to, she asked, “Where was I?” Then she told her sons, “Here shall you bury your mother.” His brother said something about how much better it would be for her to die at home, in her own country. Monica answered them both.

“Lay,” she saith, “this body any where; let not the care for that any way disquiet you: this only I request, that you would remember me at the Lord's altar, wherever you be.”

— Monica to her sons at Ostia, in Augustine's Confessions, Book IX (tr. E. B. Pusey)

Augustine heard afterward that, when he was away from the house, she had talked with some of his friends about the contempt of this life and the blessing of death. They were amazed at her courage and asked whether she was not afraid to leave her body so far from her own city. “Nothing is far to God,” she answered. In her last illness she told her son that she had never once heard a harsh or reproachful word from him against her.

She died on the ninth day of her illness, in the fifty-sixth year of her age; Augustine was thirty-three. He closed her eyes. A great sorrow rose in him, and he forced it back, so that his eyes, he wrote, “drank up their fountain wholly dry; and woe was me in such a strife!” The boy Adeodatus could not do it. He burst out into loud weeping, and the others hushed him. Then Evodius took up the Psalter and began to sing, and the whole household answered him with the psalm: “I will sing of mercy and judgments to Thee, O Lord.”

Monica had asked for one thing: to be remembered at the altar, wherever her son might be. He did not yet know where that would be. He thought he was going home to a quiet life of prayer.

Seized in the Church at Hippo

Augustine landed at Carthage about September 388 and went home to his own house and lands. For almost three years he lived there with friends who had given themselves to God as he had, in fasting, prayer, and meditation on the Scriptures day and night. Then he gave the property up. That quiet life lasted until 391.

That year a Christian at Hippo Regius, one of the imperial agents the Romans called agentes in rebus, asked to see Augustine. He was a good Christian, and Augustine went to Hippo to win him for the service of God. The man kept promising and kept putting it off.

One day, while Augustine was in the church at Hippo, the bishop needed a priest, and the people knew whom they wanted. Possidius tells what happened next: the Catholics laid hands on Augustine, “for he was standing there among the people secure and unaware of what was about to happen.” They took him to the bishop and demanded his ordination “with great zeal and clamor, while he wept freely.”

Some of the people misread the tears. They thought Augustine was hurt that they had made him only a priest, so they tried to comfort him: he deserved more, they said, but the priesthood was only a little below a bishop's office. Augustine told his friends long afterward why he had really wept. He could see the many dangers ahead. The man who had once feared that God would answer his prayer too soon had been answered in a way he had not asked for at all.

He did not pretend to be ready. How to do the work of a priest, he told Valerius in a letter, he had never learned “either in boyhood or in the earlier years of manhood.” He admitted that he had once judged the “sailors” of the Church before he had learned their work, and that he had now begun to feel “the rashness of my censures.” The office of a priest or bishop, he wrote, could be the easiest work in the world if it were done in a careless, time-serving way, but then it would be one of the most “miserable, deplorable, and worthy of condemnation in the sight of God.” He begged for a little time to prepare, “say till Easter,” and he named the way he meant to spend it: “by praying, reading, and weeping.”

Soon after his ordination he set up a monastery inside the church grounds. The rule was simple: no one owned anything of his own, and everything was held in common and given to each as he had need. Valerius, the bishop, was a Greek by birth who had never been at ease in Latin. He gave his new priest leave to preach in the bishop's own presence, which was against the custom of the African churches, and some bishops grumbled at it.

The priest soon had a chance to show what he could do. Hippo had a Manichee presbyter named Fortunatus, who had known Augustine at Carthage in the days when they shared the same beliefs. The people wanted a public debate. Fortunatus was afraid to meet his old acquaintance and agreed only when his own followers shamed him into it. On 28 August 392, at the Baths of Sossius in Hippo, the two men argued for two days. Fortunatus lost, and he left Hippo soon afterward.

Valerius watched all this with a growing fear. Other churches had no bishop. Sooner or later one of them would come for his priest.

A Bishop at a Plain Table

Valerius did not wait for it to happen. He hid his priest away, and then he wrote secretly to the primate at Carthage to ask that Augustine be made bishop of Hippo alongside him. Augustine refused. A church with a living bishop should not receive a second one, he said; it was against the custom of the Church. In the end, Possidius writes, he gave way “under compulsion and constraint.” The bishop Megalius consecrated him, about 395 or 396. Valerius died soon afterward, and Augustine was bishop of Hippo for the rest of his life.

Later he learned that a council of the Church had forbidden it. From then on he said and wrote that he should not have been ordained while his bishop was alive, and he worked to have the councils decree that ordaining bishops must make the rules known to those about to be ordained. It is a small detail, and a telling one. The man who wrote a whole book of confessions kept confessing as a bishop, even about his own appointment.

His old companions were becoming bishops too. Alypius was made bishop of Tagaste in 394, Evodius became bishop of Uzalis, and Possidius became bishop of Calama. Possidius shared Augustine's life for almost forty years, and after his death he set down, as he put it, “the things that I have seen in him and heard from him.”

He wrote down how the bishop lived from day to day. Much of each day went to lawsuits. Augustine heard cases until mealtime, and sometimes went without food all day to finish them. He kept in mind the remark of a certain man who said he would rather hear cases between strangers than between friends. With strangers, one could be won as a friend, the one in whose favor the case was justly decided. Among friends, the one who lost would be lost.

His friends often asked him to write letters on their behalf to powerful officials, and he usually refused, following the rule of a wise man of old. When he saw a real need, though, he wrote, and he wrote so well that a vicar of Africa named Macedonius answered one such letter with open admiration for his tact and wisdom.

His table was plain. There were herbs and lentils, and sometimes meat for guests or for the weaker brothers, and there was always wine. The dishes were of earthenware, wood, or marble, by his own choice and from no need, Possidius insists. His clothes followed the same rule, neither too fine nor too mean. At the table he cared more for reading and conversation than for food and drink. Possidius remembered especially the two lines of verse that Augustine had inscribed on the table, to keep out gossip.

“Quisquis amat dictis absentum rodere vitam, / Hac mensa indignam noverit esse suam.” Whoever loves to gnaw at the life of the absent with his words should know that this table is not for him.

— Verses on Augustine's table at Hippo, in Possidius, Life of Augustine, chapter 22 (our translation)

The verse was meant seriously. Once some of his closest friends among the bishops forgot it and began to talk about someone who was not there. Augustine rebuked them so sternly that he told them either the verses would have to come off the table or he would get up in the middle of the meal and go to his room. Possidius adds, as one who was there: “Both I and the others who were at the table experienced this.” The same table had a rule against oaths. Anyone who swore, even at table, lost one of his fixed number of cups of wine.

Money he kept at arm's length. He never held the key of the church's treasury or wore its ring. Others kept the accounts and read them to him once a year. He would not buy a house or an estate, and he refused gifts that would rob a man's heirs. More than once he told his people that he would rather the clergy lived on their offerings than managed church farms, and he offered to hand the properties over to them. They never accepted.

One story shows the bishop's temper on the subject. A leading citizen of Hippo, living at Carthage, gave his property to the church and kept the income for life, and Augustine thanked him. Some years later the man changed his mind. He sent his son to ask for the deeds back, with a hundred gold pieces for the poor. Augustine groaned. Either the man had only pretended to give, or he had repented of a good work. Augustine sent the deeds back at once, refused the money, and rebuked him as strongly as he could.

No woman lived in his house, not even his own sister, a widow who had led a community of women dedicated to God, nor his brother's daughters. Possidius says he never spoke with a woman except with clergy present. He taught, too, three rules he had learned from the practice of Ambrose. A man of God should never seek a wife for another man, never urge anyone to go to war, and never accept an invitation to a feast in his own community. Augustine used to praise the words Ambrose spoke on his deathbed. Those around him had begged him to pray for a longer life, and he answered them: “I have not so lived that I should be ashamed to live among you, yet I do not fear to die, for we have a Lord who is good.”

Those were good words for a bishop in Africa. The roads around Hippo were not safe for him.

The Guide Who Took the Wrong Road

Augustine's great opponents in Africa were the Donatists, a rival church with its own bishops. On their side were armed bands called Circumcellions, and Possidius says they spared neither laymen nor clergy. Once a bishop whom Augustine had sent out from his monastery fell into their ambush on the road. They took his animals and baggage and left him badly hurt.

The Circumcellions watched the roads for Augustine too. On one occasion they set an ambush on the road he was to take, and they failed to catch him. His guide lost the way, and the bishop and his companions came to their destination by another road. Only later did he learn what the mistake had saved him from. Possidius says that he gave thanks to God “together with all,” for the error had been, in fact, the providence of God.

The imperial law was against the Donatists, and one case shows how Augustine used it. Crispinus, the Donatist bishop of Calama, was told he owed the fine in gold that the civil laws set for heretics. He denied in court that he was a heretic, and a Catholic bishop was set against him in debate until he was judged one. Augustine then went to the judge and begged that the fine not be collected, and the favor was granted. Crispinus, Possidius says, ungratefully appealed to the emperor, and the emperor's answer was a decree that the Donatists should be held to the full force of all the laws against heretics. Everything was then done by the Catholic bishops, Augustine above all, to have that condemnation lifted through the emperor's indulgence, and it was.

In a homily on the first letter of John, he explained what love requires of anyone who must correct another. A father beats a boy out of love, he said, and a kidnapper strokes a boy to steal him. “If you mark the persons, it is charity that beats, iniquity that caresses.” Then he gave the short rule that people have quoted ever since, often without the sentences around it.

“Once for all, then, a short precept is given you: Love, and do what you will: whether you hold your peace, through love hold your peace; whether you cry out, through love cry out; whether you correct, through love correct; whether you spare, through love do you spare.”

— Augustine, Homily 7 on the First Epistle of John, section 8 (tr. H. Browne)

He meant correction done for love, the kind a good father gives. He did not mean permission for anything at all.

Sometimes his preaching worked in ways no one planned. One day he wandered off the subject of his sermon into a long attack on the Manichees and never got back to finish the point he had started. Not long afterward a merchant named Firmus came to the monastery and threw himself at Augustine's feet, weeping. He had been a Manichee for many years and had given the sect a great deal of money. That sermon had turned him. Augustine and his clergy asked him what part of it had moved him, and they worked out that it was the very digression. “Wondering and marvelling,” Possidius writes, they gave thanks to God, who saves souls by whatever means He wishes. Firmus gave up trade and later became a priest in another country.

In his later years Augustine also fought the Pelagians, whom Possidius calls “new heretics of our time and skilful debaters.” Against them he labored for almost ten years, writing book after book and arguing in church. African councils of bishops persuaded two popes, Innocent and then Zosimus, to condemn the teaching, and the Emperor Honorius condemned it as well.

Meanwhile the world outside the African church was coming apart. In 410 Rome itself was sacked.

Two Loves Built Two Cities

Rome had fallen to Alaric. In Alban Butler's account, it was this disaster that set Augustine to work on one of the greatest of his books. He began the City of God in 413 and finished it in 426, thirteen years of writing in the gaps of a bishop's life. Its central idea fits into a single sentence.

“Two cities have been formed by two loves: the earthly by the love of self, even to the contempt of God; the heavenly by the love of God, even to the contempt of self.”

— Augustine, City of God, Book XIV, chapter 28 (tr. M. Dods)

It was the lesson of his own life, written large across history. A people, like a person, is made by what it loves. The young man at Carthage who “loved to love” had been looking for the right thing to love all along. Even peace, he wrote, is a matter of right order, of each thing in its own place: “The peace of all things is the tranquillity of order.”

He kept asking questions, even the ones he could not answer. In the Confessions he had stopped to wonder what time is, and he gave an honest answer: “What then is time? If no one asks me, I know: if I wish to explain it to one that asketh, I know not.” He applied the same honesty to reading the Bible. Anyone who thinks he understands the Scriptures, he wrote, but finds in them a meaning that does not build up the love of God and of neighbor, “does not yet understand them as he ought.”

In the pulpit he could speak with a lighter touch. In one sermon on the Alleluia, the song of praise, he told his people how to live while they were still on the road to God. He took his picture from travelers, who sing as they walk to lighten the road.

“Quomodo solent cantare viatores; canta, sed ambula; laborem consolare cantando, pigritiam noli amare; canta et ambula.” As travelers usually sing: sing, but walk. Comfort your labor by singing. Do not love laziness. Sing and walk.

— Augustine, Sermon 256, section 3 (our translation)

Walking, he explained, meant making progress in good. Do not wander off the road, he told them, do not turn back, and do not stay behind.

He was still at work on the last book of the City of God when something new began to happen in Hippo, and he stopped to describe it.

Almost Seventy Miracles in Two Years

In 424, according to Butler, Augustine placed a portion of the relics of St. Stephen in a church at Hippo called the church of Peace. Stephen's relics had already come to other African towns. Possidius had brought some to his own city of Calama. And in the towns where the relics went, people began to report healings.

Augustine had some of those who were healed write short accounts, called libelli, and had them read aloud to the congregation, so that the people would know what had happened. When a noblewoman named Petronia was cured at Uzalis, he asked her to write her own. In the last book of the City of God he wrote that the relics had been in Hippo less than two years. Already, he said, the accounts “which have been published amount to almost seventy at the hour at which I write.” At Calama, he added, there were incomparably more.

He had known such things long before. At Milan in 386, while he was living there, a blind man had recovered his sight at the relics of the martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, which Ambrose had found. And at Carthage, soon after he came home from Italy, a cure had happened in front of him, “in my presence, and under my own eyes.”

He and Alypius, not yet clergy, were staying in the house of a former advocate named Innocentius. Their host was suffering from fistulas, and the surgeons had already operated on him once. Now they told him that a second operation was needed. The day before it, visitors came to pray with him, among them the bishop Aurelius and Saturninus of Uzalis. When they knelt, Innocentius threw himself flat on the ground and prayed with such sobs and groans that his whole body shook. Augustine knelt with the others.

“For myself, I could not pray at all,” he wrote. “This only I briefly said in my heart: O Lord, what prayers of Your people do You hear if You hear not these?” The next morning the surgeons came. The bandages were untied, and the surgeon, with his knife in his hand, searched for the wound he had come to cut. He found instead “a perfectly firm cicatrix,” a scar fully healed.

Carthage had other stories. A noblewoman named Innocentia had a cancer of the breast that her physician said could not be treated. As Easter drew near, she was told in a dream to wait at the baptistery and ask the first woman who came out newly baptized to make the sign of the cross over the sore. She did, and she was cured. When her doctor heard it, he was unimpressed, and she answered him: “What great thing was it for Christ to heal a cancer, who raised one who had been four days dead?”

Some of the stories were small and homely. In Hippo a poor old tailor named Florentius lost his coat and had no money to buy another, so he prayed aloud to the Twenty Martyrs, whose shrine stands in Hippo, to be clothed. Soon afterward he found a great fish on the shore and sold it to a cook named Catosus. When the cook cut the fish open he found a gold ring inside, and he gave it to the tailor with these words: “See how the Twenty Martyrs have clothed you.”

One of the Hippo cures, Augustine supposed, no inhabitant of the city had failed to see or hear of. It happened one Easter, about 425, in Augustine's own church. A brother and sister named Paulus and Palladia had come all the way from Caesarea in Cappadocia. Their mother had cursed them, and ever since, both had been seized with trembling. They came daily to pray at Stephen's shrine. On Easter morning, with a large crowd in the church, Paulus was holding the bars of the shrine and praying when he suddenly fell down and lay “as if asleep.” When he got up, the trembling was gone. The church filled with shouting: “Thanks to God! Praised be God!”

Two days later, Augustine had the account of Paulus's cure read to the people, while his sister stood where all could see her, still shaking. Augustine began to preach. In the middle of the sermon a new noise broke out at the shrine. Palladia had gone down to pray at the relics, and as soon as she touched the bars she collapsed in the same way as her brother “and rose up cured.” They led her into the basilica, whole. Then, Augustine wrote, “such a shout of wonder rose from men and women together, that the exclamations and the tears seemed like never to come to an end.”

The list went on. At Audurus a boy crushed under a wagon wheel was laid at the shrine and got up unhurt. In Hippo a tribune named Eleusinus laid his dead infant son on the shrine, prayed there with many tears, and took the child up alive. Augustine could have filled the rest of his book with such stories. “What am I to do?” he wrote. “I am so pressed by the promise of finishing this work, that I cannot record all the miracles I know.” His point was simple: “Even now, therefore, many miracles are wrought, the same God who wrought those we read of still performing them, by whom He will and as He will.”

He finished the City of God in 426. Within two years a new enemy came across the sea.

The Third Month of the Siege

Augustine was in his seventies now, and he did not slow down. In 428 he debated in public at Hippo with Maximinus, an Arian bishop who had come to Africa with the Gothic count Sigisvult, and the record of their exchange survives. In these last years, Possidius says, he also went back over the books he had written and corrected them.

That same year, by the reckoning of Possidius's editor, the Vandals crossed from Spain. They came by ship, with Alans and some Goths, and they overran Africa. Possidius, who had watched Augustine through so many trials, saw that he thought about this one differently from everyone else. Augustine saw cities overthrown and their people killed. Above all he saw the danger to souls, and “more than ever tears were his meat day and night.”

One bishop, Honoratus of Thiabe, wrote to ask whether bishops and clergy should leave their churches when the enemy approached. Augustine answered him in a letter, and Possidius thought the answer so necessary that he copied it whole into his life of Augustine.

Then the enemy came to Hippo. Count Boniface held the city with an army of Gothic allies, and the Vandals shut it in. According to Butler they arrived about the end of May 430. For almost fourteen months the city was besieged, even its sea-coast blockaded. Possidius and other bishops from the country around had taken refuge inside the walls, and they stayed there through the whole siege. So they were at Augustine's table, talking together about the disaster around them, when the old bishop told them what he was praying for.

“I would have you know that in this time of our misfortune I ask this of God: either that He may be pleased to free this city which is surrounded by the foe, or if something else seems good in His sight, that He make His servants brave for enduring His will, or at least that He may take me from this world unto Himself.”

— Augustine to the bishops at his table, in Possidius, Life of Augustine, chapter 29 (tr. H. T. Weiskotten)

The bishops joined him in the prayer. “And lo,” Possidius writes, “in the third month of the siege he succumbed to fever and began to suffer in his last illness.” Possidius adds: “In truth the Lord did not deprive His servant of the reward of his prayer.”

All his years as a bishop, when sick people asked him to come and pray over them and lay his hands on them, he went. Even now, people came to his bed. A man arrived with a sick relative and asked the bishop to lay his hand on him so that he would be healed. Augustine, sick himself, answered that if he had any power in such things he would surely have used it on himself first. The man told him he had had a dream, and in it he had heard these words: “Go to the bishop Augustine that he may lay his hand upon him, and he shall be whole.” When Augustine heard that, he did not delay. He laid his hand on the sick man, and, Possidius writes, “immediately God caused the sick man to depart from him healed.” Possidius knew of other such things too. More than once, when Augustine was asked to pray for people tormented by demons, he had prayed with many tears, and the demons had left them.

Augustine himself had other things on his mind. He asked that the shortest of the penitential psalms, the psalms of sorrow for sin, be copied out for him on sheets and hung on the wall where he could see them from his bed. He lay there reading them, and, Possidius says, “he wept freely and constantly.” About ten days before the end, he asked those around him to let no one in except at the hours when the doctors came or when food was brought. They did as he asked, and he had all that time for prayer.

He had preached in the church up to the very moment of this illness, Possidius says, “with a clear mind and sound judgment,” and his sight and hearing never failed him. On 28 August 430, by the traditional date, with his friends standing by, watching and praying, “he slept with his fathers.” He was seventy-six years old, and he had been a priest and a bishop for almost forty years. In their presence a service was offered to God for him, and he was buried.

He made no will. Possidius gives the reason in a single sentence: “because as a poor man of God he had nothing from which to make it.” He had helped his relatives so that they would not be in want, not so that they would be rich. He left the goods of the church in the care of the priest in charge of its buildings. And he gave one order again and again: the library of the church, and all the books, were to be carefully kept for those who would come after.

A Marble Box Under the Altar

The siege ended without him. Possidius records that Hippo was afterward abandoned by its people and burned by the enemy. The Vandals lifted the siege in July 431 and took the city by treaty a few years later. In 431, too, a letter came from the Emperor Theodosius inviting Augustine to the council at Ephesus. He had been dead for months.

He was buried, Butler says, in the church of Peace, which people had begun to call St. Stephen's after he placed the martyr's relics there. In Butler's account the Vandals, though Arians, respected his tomb and spared his library. What happened to his body next is told by later writers, and not all of their story can be proved. In Butler's version, which draws on Bede and on a ninth-century history by Oldrad, African bishops driven into exile carried the relics to Sardinia about fifty years after his death. The Augustinian historian Josef Sciberras notes that no reliable document mentions that voyage. The move to Pavia has more detail. In the 720s Liutprand, king of the Lombards, bought the relics at a high price and brought them to Pavia, in northern Italy, to the church of San Pietro in Ciel d'Oro. In 1327 the friars of the Order of St. Augustine joined the canons who already served that church, and in 1362 a marble shrine was commissioned for the relics.

In 1580 Pope Gregory XIII forbade anyone to search for the remains or move them. Then, on the morning of 1 October 1695, bricklayers working at the altar of the crypt at San Pietro lifted the paving stones and found a box of Carrara marble about four feet long. On it were letters in charcoal that were read as the name of Augustine. Inside lay a second marble box, and inside that a silver one. The find set off a long inquiry, and miracles were soon being attributed to the relics. In 1728 the bishop of Pavia declared them authentic, with a Te Deum and fireworks, and Pope Benedict XIII confirmed his judgment in writing on 22 September of that year.

When the relics were inventoried in 1884, they numbered 225 pieces of bone. They are still at Pavia, and they are shown to the faithful twice a year, on 24 April, the anniversary of his conversion, and on 28 August, his feast. In 1842 a part of the right arm was given to Bishop Dupuch for the church in Algeria. According to Wikipedia, it rests today in the arm of a marble statue in the basilica at Annaba. Pope John Paul II venerated them in 2004, when they were brought to Rome, and Pope Benedict XVI visited the shrine in April 2007.

His feast on 28 August appears in the Martyrology of Jerome and in the calendar of Carthage, which Butler counts as old as the sixth century. In 1298 Pope Boniface VIII ordered that the feasts of the four great Latin Doctors, Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, and Gregory, be kept as feasts of higher rank. OrthodoxWiki gives 15 June as his feast in the Orthodox Church, though it notes that his place in the Orthodox calendar is uncertain. A well-known story about him today is a late medieval legend, unknown to Possidius and to Augustine himself. In it, a child on a beach tells him that he will sooner empty the sea into a hole in the sand than understand the Trinity.

Possidius would not have needed it. When he finished his life of his friend, he pointed his readers to the library that Augustine had ordered kept: in those books, he wrote, “the faithful may always find him living.” Open the Confessions, and the restless young man of Carthage is still searching there. The friend is still mourning, the son is still lying to his mother on the shore, and the bishop who wrote it all down is still praying over it. In the tenth book he looked back at his whole long search and told God where the mistake had been.

“Too late loved I Thee, O Thou Beauty of ancient days, yet ever new! too late I loved Thee! And behold, Thou wert within, and I abroad, and there I searched for Thee.” And a few lines later: “Thou wert with me, but I was not with Thee.” He had looked for rest everywhere outside himself, in friends and lovers and fame and clever books, and the One he was looking for had been with him the whole time. The prayer that he had feared God would answer too soon was answered at last, in a garden in Milan. The rest that began there was completed in a besieged city, under sheets of psalms pinned to a wall. He had written the first words of his great book to God long before: “Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee.”

A Note on the Sources

The two great witnesses to Augustine's life cover different halves of it. The Confessions tell his own story up to his mother's death. Possidius, who lived beside him for almost forty years, tells of the priest and bishop and leaves out Monica and the garden in Milan entirely. These witnesses also disagree about Augustine's father. Possidius calls both parents Christian, while the Confessions and Butler say that Patricius was a pagan who was baptized only shortly before his death. Weiskotten's notes say that Megalius consecrated Augustine in 391 and also that Valerius died in 396 and Augustine succeeded him within 396–397; the Catholic Encyclopedia dates his episcopate from 396. The two statements cannot both be exact, so this life gives about 395 or 396 and treats 391 as the year of his ordination as a priest. The year of the conversion in the garden (386), the year of birth, the baptism at Easter 387, and the feast days are given as the traditional dates or as the cited editors give them. Possidius does not give the day of death; 28 August 430 comes from Prosper's chronicle as quoted by Weiskotten. No early document supports the transfer of the relics to Sardinia, according to the Augustinian postulator Josef Sciberras. The 1695 lettering is described as charcoal by the Augustinian postulator and as engraved by Butler. Augustine's Orthodox feast of 15 June and his patronages rest on OrthodoxWiki and Wikipedia only. This story tells each miracle as Possidius or Augustine reported it, and no formal Church approval of any of them was found. One tale, that Hippo was spared by his prayer, is contested, because Possidius says the city was abandoned and burned after his death.

How This Life Was Researched

This life was written from twenty sources in Latin and English. The core is the eyewitness life by Possidius, bishop of Calama, who lived with Augustine for about forty years and was in Hippo through the siege. It was read in its Latin text with Weiskotten's 1919 translation. Beside it stand Augustine's own words: the Confessions in Latin and in two public-domain English versions, three books of the City of God, a letter of 391, a sermon read in Latin, a homily, and a treatise. Butler's eighteenth-century life, the Catholic Encyclopedia, and the Augustinian postulator's history of the relics supplied the later record. The researchers flagged details that popular English pages seem to skip, among them the verses on Augustine's table, the misread tears at his ordination, and the sick man healed at his bedside, though they did not survey those pages systematically. Several sources were not read: Bede, Paul the Deacon, the letter of Oldrad, the bull of Boniface VIII, any Vatican document at its source, Baring-Gould, Guérin, Prosper's chronicle itself, the Retractationes, the Enchiridion, Sermons 340 and 169, and Letter 211.

Possidius says only that he was buried.

The Augustinian postulator Josef Sciberras notes that no reliable documents mention this transfer, and some scholars date it to the sixth or seventh century. About 720–725 Liutprand, king of the Lombards, bought the relics at a high price and brought them to Pavia, to the church of San Pietro in Ciel d’Oro. A twelfth-century story that he walked barefoot to Genoa to meet them is legend. In 1327, at the order of Pope John XXII, the Hermits of St. Augustine joined the canons who already served the church, and in 1362 a marble shrine, the Arca of St. Augustine, was commissioned.

On 1 October 1695 workmen at the crypt altar found a Carrara marble box about 120 cm long with letters read as the name of Augustine; inside were a second marble box and a silver box. Sciberras says the letters were in charcoal; Butler says the name was engraved. After a long inquiry, Bishop Francesco Pertusati of Pavia declared the relics authentic in July 1728, and Pope Benedict XIII confirmed his judgment in writing on 22 September 1728. In 1842 a part of the right arm (the cubitus) was given to Bishop Dupuch for Algeria; it is now in the basilica at Annaba, set in the arm of a marble statue. miracles.miracles:
This list gathers the wonders told about Augustine and the wonders he himself recorded, with their sources and their status. No miracle connected with Augustine has been formally approved by the Church, as far as the sources show. He was honored as a saint by popular acclaim long before the Church had formal procedures for canonization, and his feast was already kept by the sixth century. Each account below says who reported it. Most come from two witnesses: his friend Possidius, bishop of Calama, and Augustine himself, who collected the healings at the shrines of the martyrs in his own day. The list makes no claim of scientific proof, and it does not dismiss any account. Where a story is late, legendary, or contested, the entry says so.

During Augustine’s life

People tormented by demons freed at his prayer, Hippo

While Augustine was a priest and later a bishop at Hippo, he was asked more than once to pray for people tormented by demons. Possidius writes from his own knowledge that Augustine prayed for them “with many tears,” and the demons left them. Possidius gives no names or dates. All his life, when sick people asked him to come and pray over them and lay his hands on them, Augustine went.

Status: reported by Possidius, who knew Augustine for almost forty years. No formal Church approval was found.

Source: Possidius, Life of Augustine, chapters 27 and 29, translated by H. T. Weiskotten (1919), https://tertullian.org/fathers/possidius_life_of_augustine_02_text.htm

A sick man healed at his bedside, Hippo, 430

In the summer of 430, when Augustine himself lay in his last illness during the siege of Hippo, a man brought a sick relative and asked him to lay his hand on him so that he would be healed. Augustine answered that if he had any power in such things he would surely have used it on himself first. The man replied that he had heard in a dream: “Go to the bishop Augustine that he may lay his hand upon him, and he shall be whole.” Augustine then laid his hand on the sick man, and, Possidius writes, “immediately God caused the sick man to depart from him healed.” Butler repeats the story.

Status: reported by Possidius, who knew Augustine for almost forty years. No formal Church approval was found.

Source: Possidius, Life of Augustine, chapter 29, translated by H. T. Weiskotten (1919), https://tertullian.org/fathers/possidius_life_of_augustine_02_text.htm

Also in: Alban Butler, Lives of the Saints, vol. 8, “St. Augustine, Bishop, C. and Doctor,” 28 August (public domain).

An ambush escaped by a wrong turn

Armed Donatist bands called Circumcellions watched the roads for Augustine and once set an ambush on the road he was to take. His guide lost the way, and Augustine and his companions reached their destination by another road. Only later did he learn what the mistake had saved him from, and he gave thanks to God with the others. Possidius tells it as an act of God’s providence, not as a miracle.

Status: reported by Possidius as providence. No formal Church approval was found.

Source: Possidius, Life of Augustine, chapter 12, translated by H. T. Weiskotten (1919), https://tertullian.org/fathers/possidius_life_of_augustine_02_text.htm

A toothache stopped by prayer, Italy, about 386–387

In the months before his baptism, Augustine was struck by a toothache so severe that he could not speak. He wrote on a wax tablet asking the friends with him to pray for him. They knelt, and the pain stopped at once. Augustine tells the story in Book IX of the Confessions; Butler retells it.

Status: reported by Augustine about himself. No formal Church approval was found.

Source: Alban Butler, Lives of the Saints, vol. 8, “St. Augustine, Bishop, C. and Doctor,” 28 August (public domain), citing Confessions IX.4.

Monica’s dream of the wooden rule, Africa

While Augustine was still a Manichee, his mother Monica dreamed that she stood on a wooden rule and that a shining young man told her that where she was, there her son was also. Augustine suggested that the dream might mean she would come over to his side. She answered at once that she had not been told “where he, there thou also,” but “where thou, there he also.” Augustine records the dream and her answer in the Confessions; years later he joined her in the Catholic faith.

Status: reported by Augustine. A dream, not a miracle examined by the Church.

Source: Augustine, Confessions, Book III, translated by E. B. Pusey (1838), https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/3296/pg3296.txt

A child’s voice in the garden, Milan, 386 by the traditional date

Weeping under a fig tree in the garden of his house in Milan, Augustine heard from a neighboring house a voice, “as of boy or girl, I know not,” chanting again and again, “Take up and read; Take up and read.” He tried to remember whether children sang such words in any game and could not recall any. He opened the letters of Paul, read Romans 13:13–14, and “all the darkness of doubt vanished away.” Augustine does not call the voice a miracle; he tells what he heard and what followed.

Status: reported by Augustine. Not a miracle examined by the Church.

Source: Augustine, Confessions, Book VIII, chapter 12, translated by E. B. Pusey (1838), https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/3296/pg3296.txt

Hippo held out during the siege, 430–431 (contested)

Butler writes that Hippo was not taken by the Vandals during the siege and that this was “ascribed to his prayer.” The same sources also say that after the siege was lifted in July 431 the city was abandoned by its people and burned by the enemy, and the Vandals took it by treaty a few years later. Possidius, who was inside the walls, does not claim a miracle.

Status: contested. Reported by Butler only. No formal Church approval was found.

Source: Alban Butler, Lives of the Saints, vol. 8, “St. Augustine, Bishop, C. and Doctor,” 28 August (public domain); Possidius, Life of Augustine, chapter 28, translated by H. T. Weiskotten (1919), https://tertullian.org/fathers/possidius_life_of_augustine_02_text.htm

Wonders Augustine witnessed and recorded

In the last book of the City of God, Augustine set down the healings he knew of at the shrines of the martyrs, above all at the relics of St. Stephen, which had been in Hippo for less than two years when he wrote. At Hippo he had those who were healed write short accounts, called libelli, and had them read to the people. The accounts “which have been published amount to almost seventy at the hour at which I write,” he says, and at Calama there were “incomparably more.” These wonders are credited to the martyrs, not to Augustine, but he is their witness and their recorder, and they belong to his story.

A blind man sees at the relics of Gervasius and Protasius, Milan, 386

When Ambrose found the bodies of the martyrs Gervasius and Protasius at Milan, a blind man recovered his sight at their relics. Augustine was living in Milan at the time and writes that it happened while he was there, in the presence of the imperial court.

Status: reported by Augustine, who credits the healing to the relics of a martyr, not to himself. No formal Church approval was found.

Source: Augustine, City of God, Book XXII, chapter 8, translated by Marcus Dods, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/120122.htm

Innocentius healed before his second operation, Carthage

Innocentius, a former advocate at Carthage, was being treated for fistulas, and his surgeons had already operated on him once. On the day before a second operation, visitors came to pray with him, among them the bishop Aurelius and Saturninus of Uzalis. Innocentius threw himself on the ground and prayed with sobs; Augustine writes that he himself “could not pray at all.” The next morning the surgeon came with his knife in his hand and found “a perfectly firm cicatrix.” Augustine says it happened “in my presence, and under my own eyes.”

Status: reported by Augustine as an eyewitness. No formal Church approval was found.

Source: Augustine, City of God, Book XXII, chapter 8, translated by Marcus Dods, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/120122.htm

Innocentia cured of a cancer of the breast, Carthage

Innocentia, a noblewoman of Carthage, had a cancer of the breast for which her physician said there was no remedy. She was told in a dream to ask the first woman who came out of the baptistery after baptism to make the sign of the cross over the sore. She did so and was cured. When her doctor heard of it, she answered him: “What great thing was it for Christ to heal a cancer, who raised one who had been four days dead?”

Status: reported by Augustine. No formal Church approval was found.

Source: Augustine, City of God, Book XXII, chapter 8, translated by Marcus Dods, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/120122.htm

A doctor freed from gout at his baptism, Carthage

A doctor at Carthage who suffered from gout was freed from it when he was baptized. Before his baptism, Augustine was told, devils had appeared to him in a dream in the form of black boys. Augustine had the story from others.

Status: reported to Augustine by others and recorded by him. No formal Church approval was found.

Source: Augustine, City of God, Book XXII, chapter 8, translated by Marcus Dods, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/120122.htm

An old comedian cured at his baptism, Curubis

An old comedian of Curubis was cured of paralysis and of a hernia when he was baptized. Augustine writes that, at the order of Bishop Aurelius, the man was brought to Carthage so that the cure could be checked.

Status: reported by Augustine. No formal Church approval was found.

Source: Augustine, City of God, Book XXII, chapter 8, translated by Marcus Dods, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/120122.htm

A farm freed from evil spirits, Zubedi

Hesperius, who owned a farm at Zubedi, found it troubled by evil spirits. A priest offered the Eucharist there, and the trouble ceased. Hesperius kept some holy earth from Jerusalem hanging in his bedroom.

Status: reported by Augustine. No formal Church approval was found.

Source: Augustine, City of God, Book XXII, chapter 8, translated by Marcus Dods, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/120122.htm

A young man freed at the shrine of Protasius and Gervasius, Victoriana

At Victoriana, near Hippo, a young man tormented by a demon was freed at the monument of the martyrs Protasius and Gervasius.

Status: reported by Augustine, who credits the healing to the relics of a martyr, not to himself. No formal Church approval was found.

Source: Augustine, City of God, Book XXII, chapter 8, translated by Marcus Dods, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/120122.htm

A young woman freed by oil and a priest’s tears, Hippo

At Hippo a young woman tormented by a devil was freed when she was anointed with oil mixed with the tears of a priest who had been praying for her.

Status: reported by Augustine. No formal Church approval was found.

Source: Augustine, City of God, Book XXII, chapter 8, translated by Marcus Dods, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/120122.htm

Florentius the tailor and the ring in the fish, Hippo

Florentius, a poor old tailor of Hippo, lost his coat and had no money to buy another, so he prayed aloud to the Twenty Martyrs, whose shrine stands in Hippo, to be clothed. Soon afterward he found a large fish and sold it to a cook named Catosus. The cook found a gold ring inside the fish and gave it to the tailor, saying: “See how the Twenty Martyrs have clothed you.”

Status: reported by Augustine, who credits the healing to the relics of a martyr, not to himself. No formal Church approval was found.

Source: Augustine, City of God, Book XXII, chapter 8, translated by Marcus Dods, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/120122.htm

A blind woman sees, Tibilis

At Tibilis, Bishop Projectus was carrying relics of St. Stephen in procession. A blind woman received flowers that the bishop was carrying, touched them to her eyes, and saw.

Status: reported by Augustine, who credits the healing to the relics of a martyr, not to himself. No formal Church approval was found.

Source: Augustine, City of God, Book XXII, chapter 8, translated by Marcus Dods, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/120122.htm

Bishop Lucillus healed of a fistula, Sinita

Lucillus, bishop of Sinita, had suffered a long time from a fistula. He was healed while he was carrying the relics of St. Stephen in procession.

Status: reported by Augustine, who credits the healing to the relics of a martyr, not to himself. No formal Church approval was found.

Source: Augustine, City of God, Book XXII, chapter 8, translated by Marcus Dods, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/120122.htm

The priest Eucharius healed and restored to life, Calama

Eucharius, a priest from Spain living at Calama, was cured of the stone by the relics of St. Stephen that Possidius had brought to the town. Later he fell ill with another disease and lay dead, and he came back to life when the priest’s cloak, brought from the oratory, was laid on his body.

Status: reported by Augustine, who credits the healing to the relics of a martyr, not to himself. No formal Church approval was found.

Source: Augustine, City of God, Book XXII, chapter 8, translated by Marcus Dods, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/120122.htm

An old nobleman named Martial converted and baptized

Martial, an old nobleman, refused to become a Christian. His son-in-law prayed for him at the oratory of St. Stephen and took flowers from there, which were laid at the old man’s head. At dawn Martial asked for the bishop and was baptized. His last words were “Christ, receive my spirit.”

Status: reported by Augustine, who credits the healing to the relics of a martyr, not to himself. No formal Church approval was found.

Source: Augustine, City of God, Book XXII, chapter 8, translated by Marcus Dods, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/120122.htm

Two men healed of gout

Augustine adds two men healed of gout: a citizen, and a stranger who was given a cure.

Status: reported by Augustine. No formal Church approval was found.

Source: Augustine, City of God, Book XXII, chapter 8, translated by Marcus Dods, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/120122.htm

A boy crushed by a wagon wheel, Audurus

At Audurus a boy was crushed by the wheel of a wagon. He was laid at the shrine of St. Stephen and got up unhurt.

Status: reported by Augustine, who credits the healing to the relics of a martyr, not to himself. No formal Church approval was found.

Source: Augustine, City of God, Book XXII, chapter 8, translated by Marcus Dods, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/120122.htm

A woman thought dead revives, Caspalium

At Caspalium a woman was believed to be dead. Her dress was taken to the shrine of St. Stephen and brought back; when she was wrapped in it, her breath returned.

Status: reported by Augustine, who credits the healing to the relics of a martyr, not to himself. No formal Church approval was found.

Source: Augustine, City of God, Book XXII, chapter 8, translated by Marcus Dods, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/120122.htm

The daughter of Bassus the Syrian restored, Hippo

At Hippo, Bassus, a Syrian, had a daughter who died. Her dress, which had been taken to the shrine of St. Stephen, was laid on her body, and she was restored to life.

Status: reported by Augustine, who credits the healing to the relics of a martyr, not to himself. No formal Church approval was found.

Source: Augustine, City of God, Book XXII, chapter 8, translated by Marcus Dods, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/120122.htm

The son of Irenaeus the tax-gatherer revived, Hippo

At Hippo the son of Irenaeus, a tax-gatherer, died. He was anointed with the martyr’s oil and revived.

Status: reported by Augustine, who credits the healing to the relics of a martyr, not to himself. No formal Church approval was found.

Source: Augustine, City of God, Book XXII, chapter 8, translated by Marcus Dods, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/120122.htm

The infant son of the tribune Eleusinus, Hippo

Eleusinus, a tribune, laid his dead infant son on the shrine of St. Stephen, prayed there with many tears, and took the child up alive.

Status: reported by Augustine, who credits the healing to the relics of a martyr, not to himself. No formal Church approval was found.

Source: Augustine, City of God, Book XXII, chapter 8, translated by Marcus Dods, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/120122.htm

Petronia cured, Uzalis

Many miracles were reported at Uzalis, where Bishop Evodius had placed relics of St. Stephen earlier. A noblewoman named Petronia was cured there, and Augustine asked her to write her own account, a libellus, so that it could be read to the people.

Status: reported by Augustine, who credits the healing to the relics of a martyr, not to himself. No formal Church approval was found.

Source: Augustine, City of God, Book XXII, chapter 8, translated by Marcus Dods, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/120122.htm

Paulus and Palladia healed at Easter, Hippo, about 425

A brother and sister from Caesarea in Cappadocia, Paulus and Palladia, had been seized with trembling after their mother cursed them, and they came to pray daily at St. Stephen’s shrine in Hippo. On Easter Sunday morning Paulus was holding the bars of the shrine when he fell down “as if asleep,” and he rose with the trembling gone; the church shouted its thanks to God. Two days later, while the account of his cure was being read and Augustine was preaching, Palladia touched the bars, fell in the same way, “and rose up cured.” Augustine was present for both. He wrote that “such a shout of wonder rose from men and women together, that the exclamations and the tears seemed like never to come to an end.” The Oxford Cult of Saints database, which the researchers consulted only in summary, links Sermons 321–324 to these days.

Status: reported by Augustine as an eyewitness. No formal Church approval was found.

Source: Augustine, City of God, Book XXII, chapter 8, translated by Marcus Dods, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/120122.htm

A boy brought back to life, Uzalis, about 426

A sermon of Augustine, numbered 324 and dated about 426, tells of a boy brought back to life at Uzalis. The researchers knew this account only from a summary in the Oxford Cult of Saints database and did not read the sermon itself.

Status: reported by Augustine; known here only from a database summary. No formal Church approval was found.

Source: The Cult of Saints in Late Antiquity database, University of Oxford, https://portal.sds.ox.ac.uk

After Augustine’s death

Miracles attributed to the relics at Pavia, 1695–1698

On 1 October 1695, workmen at the crypt altar of San Pietro in Ciel d’Oro in Pavia found a marble box with letters read as the name of Augustine. During the inquiry that followed, Josef Sciberras, Postulator General of the Augustinian Order, writes that “a number of miracles, attributed to the relics” hastened events. No list of these miracles was found. In 1728 the bishop of Pavia declared the relics authentic, and Pope Benedict XIII confirmed his judgment; that judgment concerned the relics, not the miracles.

Status: recorded by the Augustinian Order; no details found. No formal Church approval of any miracle was found.

Source: Josef Sciberras, OSA, “The Troubled Events of the Relics of Augustine of Hippo,” https://agostinjani.org/reflections-and-articles/josef-sciberras/the-troubled-events-of-the-relics-of-augustine-of-hippo-between-transfers-findings-and-devotion/

The child at the seashore (late medieval legend)

In a well-known story about Augustine today, he walks on a beach thinking about the Trinity and meets a child pouring the sea into a hole with a spoon or a shell; the child tells him he will empty the sea sooner than Augustine will understand the Trinity. The story is not in Possidius, in the Confessions, or in the Golden Legend that Caxton translated. In 1483 Caxton wrote that he did not find it in his exemplar “neither in English, French, ne in Latin,” and had seen it painted on an altar of the Blackfriars at Antwerp. Benozzo Gozzoli painted it at San Gimignano in the fifteenth century.

Status: legendary; a late medieval tale, not history.

Source: Shari Boodts, “The Child by the Seaside: A Medieval Story about Saint Augustine,” Medievalists.net, 2019, https://www.medievalists.net/2019/02/the-child-by-the-seaside-a-medieval-story-about-saint-augustine/

teachings.teachings:
Augustine left more writing than almost any other early Christian: the Confessions, the City of God, letters, sermons, and treatises. The themes below are only a doorway. Each is given in his own words, from public-domain translations or in our own English from the Latin, with where he wrote it and how he lived it.

The restless heart

Augustine taught that people are made for God, and that nothing less than God can give them rest. Every other good thing, friendship, love, success, learning, is real and good, but it cannot carry the weight of a whole heart.

“For Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee.”

— Augustine, Confessions I.1.1 (tr. E. B. Pusey, 1838)

These are the first lines of the Confessions, which Pusey’s translation dates to about 401, when Augustine was already bishop of Hippo. The Latin says fecisti nos ad te: “you made us toward yourself,” as if the heart were always moving in one direction. He had learned it the hard way. As a young man he looked for rest in friends, in love, in rhetoric, and in the Manichees, and when a close friend died he called him “half of my soul” and found that his life had become “a horror” to him.

The divided will and the gift of grace

Augustine knew from his own life that a person can know the good and still not want it with the whole heart. He did not think that a man could heal that split by effort alone. In his own story it was healed by God, at a moment he did not choose.

“Give me chastity and continency, only not yet.”

— Augustine, Confessions VIII.7.17 (tr. E. B. Pusey, 1838)

He quoted this prayer of his youth against himself, and added: “For I feared lest Thou shouldest hear me soon.” In the garden at Milan, by the traditional date in 386, he heard a child’s voice chanting “Take up and read,” opened the letters of Paul, and found that “all the darkness of doubt vanished away.” Years later, as a bishop, he still treated his own will with suspicion: he wrote that his own consecration as bishop while his predecessor was living should not have happened, and worked to stop it from happening to others.

God within

Augustine taught that God is not found by running outward but by turning inward. He had looked for God outside himself for years, he wrote, while God was within him all along.

“Too late loved I Thee, O Thou Beauty of ancient days, yet ever new! too late I loved Thee! And behold, Thou wert within, and I abroad, and there I searched for Thee.”

— Augustine, Confessions X.27.38 (tr. E. B. Pusey, 1838)

He wrote this in the tenth book of the Confessions, looking back over his whole search. A few lines later he adds: “Thou wert with me, but I was not with Thee.” Of his years in Milan he wrote, in words we translate from his Latin, “I entered into my inmost self, with you as my guide.” In the same city he had watched Ambrose read in silence, “his voice and tongue were at rest,” and had sat with his friends in the bishop’s room for a long time, watching him, before going away.

Love is the root

For Augustine, love of God and of neighbor is the measure of everything else. Even hard acts, such as correcting someone, must grow from love. His famous short rule is not permission to do anything at all; it is a test of the heart behind an act.

“Once for all, then, a short precept is given you: Love, and do what you will: whether you hold your peace, through love hold your peace; whether you cry out, through love cry out; whether you correct, through love correct; whether you spare, through love do you spare: let the root of love be within, of this root can nothing spring but what is good.”

— Augustine, Homily 7 on the First Epistle of John, section 8 (tr. H. Browne)

He said it while preaching on the first letter of John. Just before, he had compared a father who beats a boy out of love with a kidnapper who strokes a boy to steal him: “If you mark the persons, it is charity that beats, iniquity that caresses.” He applied the same test to reading the Bible: whoever thinks he understands the Scriptures but finds in them a meaning that does not build up “this twofold love of God and our neighbor, does not yet understand them as he ought” (On Christian Doctrine I.36.40). He lived the rule as a judge: when the Donatist bishop Crispinus was fined, Augustine asked the judge not to collect the fine, and later he and the other Catholic bishops worked to have the emperor’s condemnation of the Donatists lifted.

Two loves, two cities

In the City of God Augustine taught that what a people loves makes it what it is. All of history is the story of two “cities” living side by side: one built on love of self, the other on love of God. Peace, too, is a matter of love rightly ordered.

“Two cities have been formed by two loves: the earthly by the love of self, even to the contempt of God; the heavenly by the love of God, even to the contempt of self.”

— Augustine, City of God XIV.28 (tr. M. Dods)

Butler says the sack of Rome by Alaric in 410 moved Augustine to write the City of God, which he began in 413 and finished in 426. In Book XIX he defined peace: “The peace of all things is the tranquillity of order.” He lived by the same order at his own table, where herbs and lentils were served on earthenware, wood, or marble by choice, and where two lines of verse inscribed on the table warned off anyone who loved to gossip about the absent.

Sing and walk

Augustine taught that the Christian life is a journey still under way. Christians may sing on the road, as travelers do, but they must keep going and make progress in good.

“As travelers usually sing, sing, but walk. Comfort your labor by singing. Do not love laziness. Sing and walk.”

— Augustine, Sermon 256, section 3 (our translation of “canta et ambula”)

He said it in a sermon on the Alleluia. “What does ‘walk’ mean?” he asked, and answered: make progress, make progress in good. Do not wander off the road, he told his people, do not turn back, and do not stay behind. The saying is often given as “sing and keep marching,” but the Latin ambula means “walk,” and his picture is of travelers singing to lighten the road. He had wept at the hymns of the Church in Milan after his baptism: “How did I weep, in Thy Hymns and Canticles, touched to the quick by the voices of Thy sweet-attuned Church!”

The weight of the pastor’s office

Augustine taught that being a priest or bishop is the easiest work in the world if done carelessly, and the hardest if done as God asks. He did not think anyone was simply ready for it.

“If the duties of the office of a bishop, or presbyter, or deacon, be discharged in a perfunctory and time-serving manner, no work can be in this life more easy, agreeable, and likely to secure the favour of men … but none at the same time more miserable, deplorable, and worthy of condemnation in the sight of God.”

— Augustine, Letter 21, section 1, to Bishop Valerius, 391 (NPNF tr.)

He wrote this letter in 391, soon after the people of Hippo had seized him in church and demanded his ordination while he wept. He asked Valerius for a short time, “say till Easter,” to prepare “by praying, reading, and weeping.” As bishop he heard lawsuits until mealtime and sometimes fasted all day to finish them, never held the key of the church treasury, and in a besieged city, dying, had the penitential psalms hung on his wall.

God still works wonders

Augustine taught that miracles did not end with the Apostles. God still heals, he wrote, through the prayers of his people and at the shrines of the martyrs, though such wonders are less widely known than those in the Scriptures.

“Even now, therefore, many miracles are wrought, the same God who wrought those we read of still performing them, by whom He will and as He will.”

— Augustine, City of God XXII.8 (tr. M. Dods)

He wrote this in the last book of the City of God, after collecting almost seventy written accounts of healings at the relics of St. Stephen in Hippo in less than two years. He did not claim such power for himself. When a man asked him, on his deathbed, to lay hands on a sick relative, he answered that if he had any power in such things he would have used it on himself first.

gaps: Biography: 8,318 words by the lint count; 12 block quotes; lint has no MUST FIX lines and 10 CHECK lines for long sentences, left as narrative rhythm.

The Homily 7 block quote in the biography was changed from “given thee … thou wilt” to the wording on the linked New Advent page (“given you … you will”); the notes had the older form from a secondary copy.

No source read dates the garden conversion to 386; the biography says “by the traditional reckoning.” Birth (13 Nov 354), baptism (Easter 387), and ordination (391) are the editors’ dates (Weiskotten, Butler, Catholic Encyclopedia) and are attributed in the source note.

Day of death, 28 August 430: Weiskotten’s note says Prosper’s Chronicon gives it; Prosper was not read. The biography calls it the traditional date and the source note names Weiskotten. Possidius gives only the siege month and the age.
Conflict: Possidius calls both parents Christian; the Confessions and Butler say Patricius was a pagan baptized shortly before his death (Weiskotten: 371). Told in the source note.

Conflict: Weiskotten’s notes say Megalius consecrated Augustine in 391, and also that Valerius died in 396 and Augustine succeeded him within 396–397; the Catholic Encyclopedia dates the episcopate from 396. The biography uses “about 395 or 396” and treats 391 as the ordination to the priesthood.

Orthodox feast 15 June: English Wikipedia and OrthodoxWiki (which says his place in the Orthodox calendar is uncertain); the biography attributes it to OrthodoxWiki. Patronages (theologians, sore eyes) come from English Wikipedia only and are attributed in the patron field. Brewers and printers are left out: no source found.

Misattributed lines left out: “Pray as though everything depended on God…” and “The world is a book…”. “Solvitur ambulando” not checked and not used. The Latin “Dilige et quod vis fac” was not read in a raw source, so Homily 7 is quoted in English only.
Sermo 256 is dated 5 May 418 only in a search summary; no date is given in the entry.
No formal Church approval was found for any miracle. Augustine has no formal canonization (“canonized by popular acclaim,” Wikipedia only).
The Pavia miracles of 1695–1698 are mentioned by Sciberras without a list. The boy raised at Uzalis (Sermon 324) is known only from an Oxford database summary.

Relic conflicts: Sardinia transfer undocumented; Liutprand’s purchase about 720 (Butler) or 721–725 (Sciberras); box lettering engraved (Butler) or charcoal (Sciberras); Augustinians expelled from Pavia 1785 (Wikipedia) or 1799 (Sciberras).

Not read: Bede, Paul the Deacon, Oldrad’s letter, the bull of Boniface VIII, Vatican documents at source, Baring-Gould, Guérin, Prosper’s Chronicon, the Retractationes, the Enchiridion, Sermons 169, 317–324, 340, Letter 211, Possidius ch. 9–11, 13–14, 16–17, 30.
The debate with Fortunatus (28 Aug 392) falls on the day of Augustine’s death 38 years later; no source remarks on it, so the entry does not.
No image was researched or rights-checked; three candidates are named only.
